source_read: PMC HTML, PMC3554477: abstract, Background, Prevalence and clinical presentation, Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, model section with Figure 1 legend, competing interests and authors' contributions read in full; reference list checked for the cited items (refs 43, 52-56, 60-67, 90-92, 100, 101, 107). No tables in the article.

claims.note: This narrative review supports only the core sentence: the 2009 Cochrane review (Shoptaw, Kao and Ling) found one eligible randomized trial, in which olanzapine and haloperidol were both effective (ref 92, Leelahanaj 2005, a 4-week double-blind comparison). It does not give the trial's size (58), the extrapyramidal-effect difference, the later haloperidol-quetiapine trial or the absence of placebo-controlled trials; those must come from other sources. The trial population is 'amphetamine psychosis' in the source's wording (Bramness uses 'amphetamines' for amphetamine and methamphetamine together).

anchors.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, para 4
anchors.extracted: Antipsychotics block experimentally induced amphetamine psychosis and treat amphetamine-induced psychotic symptoms; a 2009 Cochrane review (ref 91) identified only one randomized controlled trial meeting inclusion criteria (ref 92), in which olanzapine and haloperidol at clinically relevant doses were both effective. The authors add concerns that D2 blockade could worsen anhedonia and relapse risk, and mention benzodiazepines as an alternative with fewer extrapyramidal effects (no trial data given).

claims.overstatement: None from this source's side; it is itself qualitative. Note that the only number it offers on later primary psychosis ('up to 25%' after some years, ref 100, Caton et al.) concerns drug-induced psychosis across substances, not methamphetamine specifically, and that its recurrence evidence is mainly Japanese reports of spontaneous recurrence ('flashbacks') triggered by stress, i.e., recurrence without renewed use, not only with it.
claims.note: Supports the qualitative frame: faster recovery than schizophrenia with resolution on abstinence but possibly incomplete; Japanese reports of psychosis lasting up to several years and of spontaneous recurrences; up to 25% of drug-induced psychoses (all substances) later diagnosed as primary psychosis, with higher figures for methamphetamine psychosis (citing the Thai cohort, ref 67, without a number). None of the claim's figures (16-17%, 10-28%, 5% to ~39%, 19.1-30%) appear in this source.

anchors.locator: Prevalence and clinical presentation, final para
anchors.extracted: Compared with schizophrenic psychosis, amphetamine-induced psychosis seems to recover faster (refs 60-63) and to resolve with abstinence, though recovery may be incomplete (ref 43); Japanese researchers describe durations of up to several years (refs 64-66) and spontaneous relapses after remission, triggered by stress in susceptible people.

anchors.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, para 5
anchors.extracted: Up to 25% of those first diagnosed with drug-induced psychosis develop a primary psychotic disorder after some years (ref 100; all substances), with higher figures for methamphetamine-induced psychosis (ref 67, Thai long-term follow-up after first hospitalization; no figure given).

anchors.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, para 1; Prevalence and clinical presentation, para 1
anchors.extracted: A previous psychosis raises the risk of later episodes, attributed to sensitization (refs 43, 73-75); experimentally induced psychosis in early dosing studies subsided within 6 days.

claims.note: Supports 'symptoms alone do not reliably separate the two' and 'visual hallucinations may be more frequent'. The count of 12 comparison studies (1990-2017), the negative-symptom and tactile-hallucination differences, and the persistent-psychosis comparison post-date or are absent from this 2012 review and must come from other sources. This source also names more pronounced grandiosity and less prominent formal thought disorder in amphetamine psychosis, which the claim does not mention.

anchors.extracted: Symptoms of amphetamine-induced psychosis closely resemble acute schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, disorganization, lack of insight); some studies suggest more grandiosity and visual hallucinations (refs 52, 54) and less prominent formal thought disorder (ref 55); distinguishing them by acute symptoms is probably very difficult (ref 56).

reporting_issues.note: Checked against the reference list: refs 60-62 are Connell 1958 (monograph), McIver 2006 (guideline), Slater 1959 (book review); ref 90 is Leucht et al. (new vs conventional antipsychotics in schizophrenia); ref 64 is Grelotti et al. (US case report with review); ref 41 is Medhus et al. (symptom comparison in admissions), ref 43 Ujike and Sato (sensitization); ref 73 Bartlett et al. (cocaine).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low is the expected result for a debate-style narrative review; agreed that it is usable only as a statement of the vulnerability hypothesis and as a pointer to primary studies.

missed: The 'up to 25% ... after some years' figure is cited to ref 100, Caton et al., whose title describes a comparison of early-phase primary psychosis with substance-induced psychosis (Arch Gen Psychiatry), not a multi-year follow-up; the figure concerns drug-induced psychosis across substances in a US sample. Same class of citation mismatch as reporting issue 2; the encyclopedia should not attribute a methamphetamine-specific transition rate to this source.

For cl_meth_psychosis_course: Bramness's recurrence evidence is mainly Japanese reports of spontaneous, stress-triggered recurrence after remission (refs 65-70), i.e., without renewed use, plus sensitization-based risk of later episodes with use; the claim's 'recurrence with renewed use' captures only the second.

None of the specific figures in cl_meth_psychosis_course (16-17%, 10-28%, 5% to ~39%, 19.1-30%), cl_meth_psychosis_treatment (N=58, fewer extrapyramidal effects with olanzapine, later quetiapine trial) or cl_meth_psychosis_vs_schizophrenia (12 studies 1990-2017, negative and tactile symptoms) appear in this source; its anchors can support only the qualitative statements.
